title: Record Credit Card Balances Surge, McDonald’s Visits Drop: Holiday Spending Strain Looms on NBC News
body:
The United States is entering the holiday season with a financial strain that is becoming increasingly evident across a range of consumer metrics. Federal data released this week shows the personal savings rate has slipped below 4 percent of disposable income—half the level recorded before the pandemic—while credit‑card balances have surged to record highs and even routine purchases such as fast‑food meals are being postponed. Economists warn that the combination of dwindling savings, mounting debt and tepid consumer confidence could dampen holiday spending and extend the pressure into the new year.

The decline in the savings rate is the most stark indicator of the underlying vulnerability. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that the personal savings rate fell to 3.9 percent in September, the lowest point since the early 2000s. By contrast, the rate hovered around 7 percent in 2019 and peaked at more than 30 percent during the early months of the COVID‑19 pandemic when households hoarded cash amid lockdowns. Analysts attribute the current dip to a mix of higher living costs, rising energy prices and a labor market that, despite low unemployment, has not translated into real wage growth for many workers. “People are essentially living paycheck to paycheck again,” said Laura Chen, senior economist at the Center for Consumer Research. “When a sizable share of income is being used just to keep the lights on, there’s little room left for discretionary spending.”

Credit‑card debt tells a complementary story. The Federal Reserve’s latest report on consumer credit shows that revolving balances rose by $12 billion in August, pushing total credit‑card debt to a new record of $1.07 trillion. Unlike mortgage or auto loans, revolving debt is more sensitive to short‑term cash‑flow pressures because interest accrues monthly and balances can quickly become unmanageable. The surge is being driven largely by everyday expenses—groceries, utilities and transportation—rather than large, one‑off purchases. “What we’re seeing is a shift from savings to borrowing to cover routine costs,” noted Mark Alvarez, a credit‑union analyst in Chicago. “That’s a red flag for consumer resilience, especially when holiday shopping traditionally adds another layer of spending.”

Even low‑cost indulgences are feeling the pinch. Data from a national fast‑food chain indicates that visits to its outlets fell by 5 percent in the first half of September, the steepest decline in a decade. While the chain did not disclose exact figures, industry observers link the dip to tighter household budgets and a broader trend of “frugal living” that has taken hold since the midterm elections, when economic issues dominated the political conversation. The reduction in casual dining is symptomatic of a larger pullback on non‑essential expenditures, which could translate into lower sales for retailers that rely on impulse purchases.

The holiday shopping season, historically a boost for the economy, may therefore be muted. Retail analysts project that total holiday sales could grow by only 2‑3 percent this year, a slowdown from the 5‑6 percent gains seen in recent years. Some retailers are already adjusting their strategies, offering deeper discounts earlier in the season and promoting financing options that could further inflate credit‑card balances. However, the risk of over‑extension remains high; a surge in defaults after the holidays could erode consumer confidence even more.

Looking ahead, policymakers face a delicate balancing act. The Federal Reserve is expected to maintain its current interest‑rate stance for the near term, but any further hikes could exacerbate borrowing costs and strain already stretched households. Meanwhile, fiscal measures aimed at bolstering disposable income—such as targeted tax credits or expanded unemployment benefits—could provide temporary relief but may not address the structural issues of wage stagnation and rising living costs. As families navigate the upcoming holidays, the interplay between savings, debt and consumer confidence will be a critical barometer of economic health, shaping not only the season’s retail performance but also the broader trajectory of the U.S. economy in the months to come.
